title: Portuguese grammar
intro: A working reference for beginners to intermediate learners, with Brazilian usage first and Portugal's differences noted. Every pattern comes with real sentences and a translation: read a section, notice the shape, then listen for it in what you watch and read.

sections.title: Nouns, articles & gender
sections.text: Most nouns in **-o** are masculine and most in **-a** feminine; **-ção, -dade, -gem** are feminine (a canção, a cidade, a viagem). Plurals: add **-s**; **-ão → -ões** (usually), **-l → -is** (animal → animais), **-m → -ns** (homem → homens). Prepositions merge with articles: **de + o = do, em + a = na, a + o = ao, por + o = pelo**.

examples.translation: The price of bread went up.

sections.title: Pronouns, você & tu, a gente
sections.text: In Brazil **você** (with the third-person verb) is the normal "you"; in Portugal **tu** is used with friends and **você** can sound distant (people use the name or o senhor / a senhora). In everyday Brazilian speech **a gente** replaces nós and takes the singular verb: **A gente vai.**

sections.title: Present tense (regular verbs)
sections.rule: Drop -ar, -er or -ir and add the ending for the person.
sections.text: For "right now": Brazil uses **estar + gerund** (**estou comendo**), Portugal **estar a + infinitive** (**estou a comer**). Both are understood everywhere.

sections.title: ser vs. estar (and ficar)
sections.text: For the permanent location of buildings and places Portuguese often uses **ficar**: **Onde fica o banco?** (Where is the bank?). ficar also means "to become" or "to stay": **Fiquei feliz** (I was happy), **Fica aqui** (Stay here).

head: ser
estar
rows: Ela é médica. | She's a doctor. ;; São três horas. | It's three o'clock.
Estou cansado. | I'm tired. ;; Ele está em casa. | He's at home.

examples.text: Sou do Brasil, mas estou em Lisboa.
examples.translation: I'm from Brazil, but I'm in Lisbon.

sections.title: Key irregular verbs
sections.text: Also common: **querer** (quero, quer), **dizer** (digo, diz), **ver** (vejo, vê), **vir** (venho, vem), **saber** (sei, sabe), **dar** (dou, dá). **ter que + infinitive** = to have to: **Tenho que trabalhar.** **ir + infinitive** is the everyday future.

sections.title: Negation & questions
sections.text: **não** goes before the verb, and double negatives are correct: **Não vi ninguém.** Questions usually keep normal word order with a rising voice. In Brazil **né?** (não é?) ends many sentences. "Why" is **por que** in a question and **porque** in the answer (Portugal: porque in both).

head: Example
rows: Nunca como carne. ;; Não vi nada. ;; Não tem ninguém.
onde | where ;; quando | when ;; como | how ;; por que | why ;; quanto | how much ;; quem | who ;; o que | what
Você vem, né? | You're coming, right?

sections.title: Pretérito perfeito (what happened)
sections.text: This is the simple past for completed actions; Portuguese doesn't use a "have done" tense for this. **ir** and **ser** share the same forms (fui = I went / I was). Other irregulars: **ter → tive, teve; fazer → fiz, fez; estar → estive, esteve; poder → pude, pôde; dizer → disse**.

examples.translation: We went to the beach on Saturday.

sections.title: Imperfeito vs. pretérito perfeito
sections.text: Irregular imperfeito: **ser → era, ter → tinha, vir → vinha, pôr → punha**. The imperfeito is also a polite present: **Queria um café** (I'd like a coffee).

head: imperfeito
pretérito perfeito
rows: Chovia muito. | It was raining a lot. ;; Quando era criança, jogava futebol. | As a child I used to play football.
O telefone tocou. | The phone rang.

examples.text: Eu estava lendo quando você ligou.
examples.translation: I was reading when you called.

examples.text: Aos domingos íamos à casa da minha avó.
examples.translation: On Sundays we used to go to my grandmother's.

examples.text: Queria saber o horário do ônibus.
examples.translation: I'd like to know the bus timetable.

sections.title: Object pronouns & their position
sections.text: Brazil puts pronouns **before the verb** (**Me dá o livro**, **Eu te amo**) and in speech often uses ele / ela as objects (**Vi ele ontem**). Portugal puts them **after the verb with a hyphen** in plain statements (**Dá-me o livro**, **Vi-o ontem**) but before it after negations and question words (**Não o vi**). After an -r infinitive, o / a become **lo / la**: **Vou fazê-lo.**

sections.title: The subjunctive
sections.text: Present subjunctive: take the eu form, drop -o, swap the vowel (falo → **que eu fale**, como → **que eu coma**). Irregular: **ser → seja, estar → esteja, ir → vá, ter → tenha, fazer → faça**. Portuguese also has a **future subjunctive** after quando, se, assim que about the future: **Se der, eu vou** (If it works out, I'll go).

head: Example
rows: Espero que você venha. | I hope you come.
Se eu tivesse tempo, viajaria. | If I had time, I'd travel.
future: when / if about the future
Quando você chegar, me avisa. | When you arrive, let me know.

examples.text: É melhor que a gente saia agora.
Se eu fosse você, não faria isso.
examples.translation: If I were you, I wouldn't do that.

examples.text: Assim que puder, eu te ligo.
examples.translation: As soon as I can, I'll call you.

sections.title: Comparing
sections.text: **melhor** works as both "better" (adjective) and "better" (adverb): **Este é melhor. Ela canta melhor.**

head: Pattern
Example
rows: São Paulo é maior que o Rio.
Ele é tão alto quanto eu.
bom → melhor ;; mau → pior ;; grande → maior ;; pequeno → menor

examples.text: O metrô é mais rápido do que o ônibus.
examples.translation: The metro is faster than the bus.

examples.text: É o melhor restaurante do bairro.
examples.translation: It's the best restaurant in the neighbourhood.

sections.title: One-page memory map
points: Learn o or a with every noun; prepositions merge with articles (do, na, ao, pelo).
você (+ 3rd-person verb) is the Brazilian 'you'; tu in Portugal; a gente = we in speech.
ser for what something is; estar for states; ficar for where places are.
ir + infinitive is the everyday future.
Pretérito perfeito tells what happened; imperfeito paints the background and habits.
Brazil: pronoun before the verb (me dá); Portugal: after with a hyphen (dá-me).
Double negatives are correct: não vi ninguém.
The subjunctive follows que after wishes and doubt; se + imperfect subjunctive for imagined situations.
quando / se about the future take the future subjunctive: quando você chegar.
sections.tip: Listening strategy: vowels shrink in unstressed syllables, especially in Portugal (telefone → "tlfon"). Hold on to the stressed syllable and the verb ending, and the nasal sounds (-ão, -em, -im) that mark many endings.
